guide.title: About 3G2 files
guide.markdown:
### What is a 3G2 file?

3G2 is a video container defined by 3GPP2, the standards group behind CDMA mobile networks, for clips shot and sent on phones. It uses the ISO media file format family as its foundation, and RFC 4393 registered its media types in March 2006. The preferred extension is .3g2, and .3gpp2 is also recognized.

A 3G2 can carry sound, moving pictures and timed text. The type video/3gpp2 is valid even when the file holds only audio, while audio/3gpp2 is reserved for files with nothing visual, and timed text counts as visual content. So a 3G2 that plays without a picture is not always broken.

You meet these files on older CDMA phones and in their MMS video. The format keeps files small, and its video is H.264 or MPEG-4. Recognizing the container does not guarantee that a player has a decoder for the video or sound inside it, which is the usual reason a 3G2 opens on one device and not on another.

### Programs that open 3G2 files

VLC media player and QuickTime Player both open 3G2 clips. These programs also handle the format:

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- FFmpeg: registers .3g2 with its QuickTime and ISO base media demuxer.
- ffplay: the FFmpeg player, which uses the FFmpeg demuxers and decoders.

**Windows and Mac**

- Adobe After Effects: recognizes .3g2 as an import extension.

### 3G2 and MP4 compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .3g2 or .3gpp2 with video/3gpp2, where audio/3gpp2 is kept for files with nothing visual; .mp4 for MPEG-4 Part 14.
- **Standards**: 3G2 comes from 3GPP2 and is based on the MPEG-4 container. MP4 is defined in ISO/IEC 14496-14.
- **Video codecs**: a 3G2 holds H.264 or MPEG-4 video. MP4 takes H.264, H.265 and AV1.
- **Extras**: MP4 can carry subtitles and chapters.
- **Reach**: MP4 plays on nearly every device. The older 3G2 is kept small and was made for phones.

What this page does is decode the clip and write a new MP4. The picture is re-encoded by x264 using CRF 32 and its ultrafast preset, while the soundtrack is re-encoded as 96 kbps AAC. An oversized picture is scaled down to 1920 pixels along its longer edge, and playback speed tops out at 30 frames per second. Your 3G2 itself is never changed; you download a new file next to it.

Conversion happens in your browser, one clip at a time, with no file-size cap from the page. Pick several files and they queue, each saved under its own name with the .mp4 ending. No stream-selection options are passed, which leaves FFmpeg's defaults to pick the streams that reach the MP4. An audio-only 3G2 gives an MP4 with sound and no picture.

### Other ways to convert 3G2 to MP4

- **FFmpeg with a re-encode:** on Windows, Mac or Linux, run `ffmpeg -i handset.3g2 -c:v libx264 -c:a aac handset-share.mp4`. It encodes video with libx264 and audio with aac, and the result is lossy.
- **FFmpeg, copy the streams:** run `ffmpeg -i archive-phone.3g2 -c copy archive-phone.mp4`. Nothing is re-encoded, but it works only when MP4 accepts the streams inside.
- **Prism (Windows):** click Add File(s), set Output Format to MP4, check Encoder Options, pick a folder under Save to Folder and click Convert. NCH lists 3G2 input for Windows only.

### Problems with 3G2 files

- **No picture**: a video/3gpp2 file may be audio only, so a missing picture is not always a playback failure.
- **Won't play on a phone or in an editor**: the app in question may not have a decoder for the picture or sound stored in the file. Converting here writes new H.264 and AAC streams, provided FFmpeg can decode the original.
- **Corrupt after a transfer**: a text-style transfer that changes line endings or strips high bits can corrupt this binary format.
- **A damaged or cut-short clip**: a clip like this usually still converts, giving a shorter MP4, so compare the running time with the original.
- **A soft or blocky result**: encoding uses CRF 32 with the ultrafast preset and offers no quality control, so the MP4 can look worse than the 3G2.
- **An odd .3gpp2 ending**: it is the second registered extension for the same format. Rename it to .3g2 if a program only looks for that one.

guide.title: About AVI files
guide.markdown:
### What is an AVI file?

Windows 3.1 got AVI, short for Audio Video Interleave, from Microsoft, with a first specification from 1992. Pictures and sound that run on a timeline are stored in a RIFF file. One chunk holds the header (dimensions, frame rate and similar), another holds the media, and FOURCC codes name each stream and codec.

Uncompressed, lossless or lossy video can all live in an AVI, so the extension alone cannot tell you its quality or size. The usual ending is .avi, and one common media-type label is video/x-msvideo.

You find AVI in video production archives and in older desktop workflows such as camera and capture output. It is a legacy container, and people often replace it with something newer.

### Programs that open AVI files

QuickTime Player, VLC and Windows Media Player all play AVI. Sorted by platform, the fact sheet for AVI names these programs:

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- ffplay: FFmpeg contains the AVI demuxer.
- mpv: desktop playback where audio and subtitle streams are selectable.

**Windows and Mac**

- Adobe Premiere: takes in the container so long as the decoder it needs is there.

**Mobile**

- VLC for Android and VLC for iOS: the Android app is free, and what it decodes follows from the contents of the container; the iOS app is a mobile player that handles most movie formats and reaches both local and network media.

### AVI and MKV compared

- **Names and types**: .avi is commonly labeled video/x-msvideo, and IANA registers video/matroska for Matroska video.
- **Structure**: AVI is built from RIFF chunks. Matroska rests on EBML, a binary structure that derives from XML.
- **Tracks**: Matroska can carry several video, audio and subtitle streams, and chapters and descriptive tags are part of its design. AVI has limited support for modern features.
- **Codecs**: no codec or quality level is built into either container. An AVI may hold uncompressed, lossless or lossy video, and Matroska leaves the compression method open.
- **Origins**: Microsoft introduced AVI in 1992. Matroska developed from the earlier MCF project.

This page does not just rewrap the AVI. It decodes the video and writes it again through x264 at CRF 32 with its ultrafast preset, writes the sound as 96 kbps AAC, scales anything past 1920 pixels along the longer edge, and holds the rate to 30 fps. The MKV is a compressed copy, not an archival match of the AVI, and you cannot change the quality.

No stream mapping is passed, so FFmpeg's own defaults pick the streams, and its defaults also copy global tags where the output can hold them. For a plain one-video, one-audio AVI that is what you expect. Your original stays untouched, and the download is named after the AVI with the .mkv ending. Pick several files and they convert in turn, one MKV each. This page does not cap the size.

### Other ways to convert AVI to MKV

- **FFmpeg, remux (Windows, Mac, Linux):** run `ffmpeg -i capture-master.avi -c copy capture-master.mkv`. Streams are copied without re-encoding, and FFmpeg chooses them automatically.
- **HandBrakeCLI:** run `HandBrakeCLI --input avi-review.avi --output avi-review.mkv --format av_mkv --encoder x264 --aencoder av_aac --quality 22`. This re-encodes, so it is a derivative copy.
- **Prism (Windows):** add the AVI, set Output Format to MKV, review Encoder Options, set Save to Folder and click Convert. Its available codecs depend on the installation.

### Problems with AVI files

- **The player opens it but an editor rejects it**: an editor may identify AVI yet have no decoder for what is actually inside.
- **A huge capture won't open**: the original AVI design limits size in ways the later OpenDML extension does not, so big captures need software that copes.
- **Stretched or combed picture**: implementations of AVI do not treat aspect ratio and scan type in a consistent way. Check the MKV in a player.
- **Wrong or missing extra track**: this page does not map tracks, and FFmpeg's defaults decide. Run FFmpeg yourself if you need a specific stream layout.
- **A damaged or cut-short AVI**: it often converts anyway, yielding a shorter MKV. Compare its running time with the source.
- **A smaller picture than the source**: this page scales footage whose longer side passes 1920 pixels. The FFmpeg remux keeps the original size.
- **A soft or blocky result**: the page re-encodes at CRF 32 with the ultrafast preset, so the MKV can look worse than the AVI.

guide.title: About AVI files
guide.markdown:
### What is an AVI file?

With Windows 3.1, Microsoft brought out Audio Video Interleave; the first specification followed in 1992. A RIFF file stores the timed pictures and sound, and a header in it notes things like size and frame rate. Another chunk contains the media, and FOURCC identifiers label every stream and codec.

Because the container leaves the codec open, the video inside can be uncompressed, lossless or lossy, and the .avi ending reveals nothing about quality. A commonly used media-type label is video/x-msvideo.

AVI turns up in archived footage and in old Windows video, whether camera or capture output. It is a legacy format with limited support for modern features.

### Programs that open AVI files

AVI opens in Windows Media Player, QuickTime Player and VLC. By platform, the format's fact sheet adds:

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- ffplay: the AVI demuxer ships with FFmpeg.
- mpv: desktop player where you select audio and subtitle streams.

**Windows and Mac**

- Adobe Premiere: opens the container provided the required decoder is present.

**Mobile**

- VLC for Android and VLC for iOS: on Android it is free, and whether a file decodes hinges on the media inside the container; on iOS it is a phone and tablet player for most movie formats, covering local files and network media.

### AVI and WebM compared

- **Labels**: .avi is commonly tagged video/x-msvideo. WebM video uses video/webm, and an audio-only WebM uses audio/webm.
- **Structure**: AVI is RIFF chunks. WebM is based on Matroska, which is built on EBML.
- **Codecs**: AVI may hold uncompressed, lossless or lossy video. For WebM the picture is VP8 or VP9 (AV1 video is allowed too), with Vorbis or Opus as the sound.
- **Licensing**: the WebM Project supplies its format technology under royalty-free terms.
- **Browser reach**: major browsers support WebM, and Chrome, Firefox and Edge open it.
- **Age**: Microsoft introduced AVI in 1992, and WebM is an open format promoted for web delivery.

This page decodes the AVI and writes a new WebM. The video is VP8 from libvpx at CRF 40 in its realtime mode with the fastest CPU setting, written as 8-bit yuv420p. The sound is Vorbis at 64 kbps. A picture past 1920 pixels along its longer edge is scaled down, and a quicker source is thinned to 30 frames per second without changing how long it lasts. The settings favor speed over detail, so keep the AVI if quality may matter later.

FFmpeg's defaults decide which streams go in, since nothing is mapped by hand. Your AVI is never changed, and the download is named after it with the .webm ending. The page applies no size limit, so a long file simply keeps a slower device busy for longer. Pick several files and they convert in turn.

### Other ways to convert AVI to WebM

- **FFmpeg on a desktop:** run `ffmpeg -i web-source.avi -c:v libvpx-vp9 -b:v 1024k -crf 32 -c:a libopus web-delivery.webm` for VP9 and Opus in constrained-quality mode, which Google's VP9 guide recommends for on-demand video. The result is lossy.
- **HandBrake (Windows, Mac, Linux):** choose the AVI under Open Source, then set the container to WebM. HandBrake lists VP8, VP9 and AV1 video encoders for WebM, with Vorbis or Opus audio.
- **Prism (Windows):** add the file, choose WebM as the output, set the encoder and folder, then click Convert. NCH lists AVI as an input and WebM as an output.

### Problems with AVI files

- **An editor shows black frames or silence**: an editor can know AVI and still have no decoder for the specific contents.
- **Two AVI files look nothing alike**: the file name does not reveal quality, since the contents may be uncompressed, lossless or lossy.
- **The WebM looks soft in motion**: the page trades detail for speed. The FFmpeg command above uses VP9 and a quality target instead.
- **The WebM plays in one browser and not another**: what plays is set by the real video and audio codecs, and the .webm suffix alone settles nothing.
- **Seeking feels slow**: without a cue index, seeking can be less efficient, since the player has less direct information about where things are.
- **An old Safari will not play it**: macOS Safari gained WebM playback in version 14.1 for VP8 or VP9 video with Vorbis sound, so do not assume older releases play it.
- **Wrong picture shape**: AVI implementations differ in how they treat aspect ratio and scan type. Check the result in a player.
- **A very large AVI fails to open**: the first AVI design has size restrictions that the later OpenDML extension does not, so large captures need compatible software.
- **A damaged or cut-short AVI**: it commonly converts all the same, giving a shorter WebM. Compare its running time with the source.

guide.title: About BMP files
guide.markdown:
### What is a BMP file?

BMP, the Windows Bitmap, is Microsoft's raster image family, used originally on Windows and OS/2. Windows 98 brought the fifth version in 1998, which is able to carry both an ICC profile and an alpha channel. The registered media type is image/bmp.

Pixels in a BMP are usually stored uncompressed, with run-length encoding as an optional lossless alternative. That makes the format simple to read and write, but it produces large files. Depth runs from 1 to 32 bits per pixel.

Most BMP files are Windows screen captures or system graphics; the format also serves plain Windows artwork and image exchange without compression. Microsoft controls the format, and the Library of Congress documents it among the formats it follows for preservation.

### Programs that open BMP files

Windows Paint, Windows Photos, Preview on macOS and GIMP all open BMP. Further programs, from the format's fact sheet:

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- ImageMagick: reads BMP images, which the magick command can then write out as JPEG.
- XnView MP: BMP is among its supported image formats, and company use requires a license.

**Web**

- Firefox: shows BMP pictures inside web content.
- Google Chrome: BMP images are supported, per Mozilla's browser compatibility table.

### BMP and JPEG compared

- **Names and types**: .bmp is image/bmp. A JPEG may end in .jpg or in .jpeg.
- **Compression**: BMP commonly stores raw pixels, with lossless compression as an option. JPEG is lossy and designed for photographs.
- **Transparency**: BMP version 5 can store an alpha channel. JPEG has no alpha transparency.
- **Color depth**: BMP spans 1 to 32 bits per pixel. This page's JPEG comes from a browser canvas with 8 bits per channel.
- **Metadata**: a BMP can carry an ICC profile from version 5. This page does not copy it.
- **Typical use**: BMP serves simple Windows graphics and uncompressed image interchange. Web photographs, camera files, email attachments and shared photos are typically JPEGs.
- **Standard**: ISO/IEC 10918-1 specifies JPEG, a format that the Joint Photographic Experts Group created. Microsoft controls the BMP family.
- **Quality**: JPEG normally has an adjustable quality. This page fixes it at 0.85 and shows no slider.

The page asks your browser to decode the BMP with its own image decoder, then encodes a JPEG at quality 0.85 from a canvas. The picture goes through raw pixels with 8 bits per channel, so only the pixels survive: tags, an embedded ICC profile and any transparency are left behind. You get a single still picture, and the conversion runs on your own device with no server involved. The page imposes no size limit, and the BMP you started with stays as it was. A multi-file selection runs file after file, giving one JPEG per BMP, named like the BMP but ending .jpeg.

### Other ways to convert BMP to JPEG

- **GIMP on any desktop:** open the BMP, then pick File > Export As. A JPEG export dialog then lets you set the quality from 0 to 100, with a default of 85.
- **ImageMagick (command line):** run `magick scan-bitmap.bmp -quality 90 scan-photo.jpeg`. The -quality option takes 1 to 100, so you pick the quality yourself, which this page never lets you do.

### Problems with BMP files

- **The BMP takes up too much space**: an uncompressed BMP can be large, so PNG or JPEG may suit distribution better.
- **Transparency turned into something else**: JPEG cannot hold transparent pixels. Use the [BMP to PNG converter](/bmp-to-png/) if you must keep see-through areas.
- **A decode error from this page**: the browser could not read the file, which suggests damage or a file that is not truly a BMP.

guide.title: About CAF files
guide.markdown:
### What is a CAF file?

CAF, Core Audio Format, is a container Apple designed as a flexible home for audio. Core Audio support dates to OS X 10.4, with OS X 10.3 support through QuickTime 7. Where older containers use small size fields, CAF uses 64-bit offsets, so it has no 4 GB ceiling.

A CAF can hold compressed audio or uncompressed samples, with multiple channels and optional channel-layout information. A mandatory audio-description chunk identifies the stored audio encoding, and information and edit-comment chunks can carry descriptive text.

You meet CAF as audio on macOS and iOS, as long recordings and as sound effects in Apple apps. Many codecs fit inside it, so two CAF files can hold very different audio, and the format is also described as supporting metadata and markers. It is an Apple format.

### Programs that open CAF files

QuickTime Player, Apple Music, Logic Pro and Audacity open CAF files. The format's fact sheet adds these programs:

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- FFmpeg: handles Core Audio Format containers in both directions.
- ffplay: uses FFmpeg demuxers and decoders to play supported CAF audio.

### CAF and WAV compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .caf for CAF; .wav for WAV, with audio/wav and audio/x-wav as common media-type labels.
- **Origin**: CAF is Apple's format. WAV comes from a Microsoft and IBM multimedia specification of August 1991.
- **Structure**: CAF uses 64-bit offsets. WAV is a RIFF-based wrapper for sound rather than one particular audio encoding.
- **Contents**: a CAF can hold compressed or uncompressed audio. WAV often holds linear PCM, though compressed encodings are possible as well.
- **Size limit**: CAF has no 4 GB limit. WAV has a 4 GB file size limit.
- **Metadata**: CAF has information and edit-comment chunks. What a WAV does with metadata varies, as INFO chunks and the Broadcast WAVE extensions store different details.
- **Typical use**: WAV serves audio recording and editing and professional sound production.

WAV, short for Waveform Audio File Format, is a RIFF-based sound wrapper described in the multimedia specification Microsoft and IBM published in August 1991. It usually holds uncompressed PCM audio, so files are large but exact. Broadcast WAVE carries production and preservation metadata. The Library of Congress names WAVE its recommendation for digital audio collections.

The conversion is a decode and rewrite. FFmpeg in your browser reads the CAF and writes 16-bit little-endian PCM into a WAV, dropping any video stream. The page passes no quality setting. No tag options are passed either; FFmpeg's defaults decide, and in a test the CAF's title and artist arrived in the WAV. The CAF stays unchanged, and the download takes its name with a .wav ending. A batch of CAF files runs in sequence and yields a separate WAV for each.

### Other ways to convert CAF to WAV

- **FFmpeg (Windows, Mac, Linux):** run `ffmpeg -i field-recording.caf -c:a pcm_s16le field-edit.wav`. 16-bit output can reduce the source depth.
- **Switch (Windows):** add the CAF, choose WAV as the output format, set the encoder options and an output folder, then click Convert. NCH lists CAF input and WAV output for Windows, Mac and Android versions of the program.

### Problems with CAF files

- **It opens but there is no sound**: opening the container does not guarantee that a system can decode the audio codec inside it.
- **The channel layout is not what you expected**: CAF can hold optional channel-layout information. Check the channel order in your editor after converting a multichannel recording.
- **A 24-bit recording loses depth**: the page writes 16-bit PCM, so a deeper CAF is reduced to 16 bits.
- **The WAV is much larger than expected**: the CAF held compressed audio, and PCM is uncompressed.
- **CAF notes are missing from the WAV**: information and edit-comment chunks in a CAF can carry descriptive text, but this page promises only what FFmpeg's defaults copy, such as global tags. Check the WAV in your editor if the notes matter.
- **A program cannot open the CAF at all**: FFmpeg reads and writes the Core Audio Format container, so it can turn the file into a WAV from the command line, and ffplay can play supported CAF audio.
- **A damaged or cut-short CAF**: such a file usually still converts, giving a shorter WAV, so compare its running time with the CAF.

### What is a CDR file?

The default drawing format of CorelDRAW is CDR. Corel calls it a primarily vector format: instead of a grid of pixels, the drawing is kept as shapes, curves, text and effects, across multiple pages and layers. Bitmap content can sit inside a drawing next to vector effects, and the save options offer compression for bitmaps and for graphic objects.

Properties like a title and subject can be stored in a CDR, and fonts can be embedded where permissions and other restrictions allow. In the Save As dialog you can pick an earlier CDR version for compatibility, which matters because an older CorelDRAW may reject a drawing from a newer one.

You meet CDR files as logos, illustrations, signage and print design. CDR is a proprietary Corel format, and LibreOffice Draw and Inkscape read it through libcdr.

The target, JPEG, is a raster format with lossy compression, which the Joint Photographic Experts Group specified as ISO/IEC 10918-1. Web photographs, camera files, mailed attachments and shared pictures commonly use it, and its quality can be adjusted.

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- LibreOffice Draw: imports CDR through libcdr.

**Windows and Mac**

- CorelDRAW: opens its native drawings.

**Web**

- The web edition, CorelDRAW Web: documentation covers CDR support in compatible browsers; qualifying Graphics Suite subscribers and maintenance customers get access as a benefit.

### CDR and JPG compared

- **Names and types**: .cdr is CorelDRAW's native format. JPEG files end in .jpg or .jpeg, which mean the same thing.
- **Kind**: CDR is primarily vector. JPEG is a raster format designed for photographs, so shapes become pixels.
- **Compression**: JPEG is lossy, with no alpha transparency, so transparent pixels cannot survive a JPEG export.
- **Pages and layers**: a CDR can have multiple pages and layers. JPEG is one flat raster picture with no editable layers, so keep your CDR.
- **Support**: a JPEG is supported everywhere, and you can view it in Windows Photos, GIMP, Preview on macOS or a browser. A CDR opens in CorelDRAW, LibreOffice Draw and Inkscape.

Once the drawing is a JPG its vector shapes are pixels, so pick the export size you need before saving, because enlarging the JPG afterwards cannot restore sharp edges.

LibreOffice Draw can export to any of the graphics formats BMP, EMF, EPS, GIF, JPEG, PNG, SVG, TIFF and WMF. CorelDRAW itself offers JPEG in its export dialog, with options for the current page or only the selected objects.

### Other ways to convert CDR to JPG

- **CorelDRAW on Windows or Mac:** open the drawing, choose File > Export, set Save as type to JPEG, type a file name, optionally tick Export this page only or Selected only, and click Export.
- **LibreOffice Draw on Windows, Mac or Linux:** open the CDR, then export it as JPEG. LibreOffice's guide lists JPEG among the graphics formats Draw exports and Corel Draw (*.cdr) among the formats it opens.

- **An older CorelDRAW will not open it**: the drawing was probably saved by a newer version. Ask for a copy saved in an earlier version, which the newer program offers.

DXF is used to exchange CAD drawings, for CNC, laser cutting and plotting work, and for architectural and engineering drawings. It carries 2D and 3D geometry and layers.

JPEG is the output here: a raster image format with lossy compression, the Joint Photographic Experts Group standardized it in ISO/IEC 10918-1. It fits web photos, pictures from cameras, emailed attachments and photo sharing, with a quality that can be set.

tool.subtitle: This converter has no EMF reader. Use Inkscape, LibreOffice Draw or ImageMagick to make the PNG.

faqs.question: Can I convert EMF to PNG on this page?
faqs.answer: No: this page ships without any EMF reader. The browser's decoder receives the file and in a test failed on an EMF, so the page shows 'Image decode failed.' Pick a program from the guide below.

faqs.question: What is the easiest way to turn an EMF into a PNG?
faqs.answer: Open it in Inkscape and choose File > Export PNG Image. LibreOffice Draw can open an EMF and export it as PNG too.

faqs.question: Is there a command-line way?
faqs.answer: ImageMagick lists EMF as readable on Windows only, with the size option supported, so the plain two-file magick command from the first method below is the one to use there.

faqs.question: Where do EMF files come from?
faqs.answer: EMF records Windows GDI drawing commands. Windows and Microsoft Office use it to embed graphics, among them pasted charts and diagrams, printing output and clipboard content.

faqs.question: Will the PNG keep the picture sharp?
faqs.answer: Only at the size you export. EMF records drawing commands and keeps drawing proportions across output devices, while a PNG is a fixed grid of pixels.

faqs.question: Why does the picture look different from the original?
faqs.answer: Import support does not establish complete fidelity. Inkscape warns that some imported formats lose unsupported features, and an older EMF reader may not implement newer records.

faqs.question: Can an EMF contain a bitmap?
faqs.answer: Yes. An EMF can contain bitmaps next to its drawing records, so one file may mix both kinds.

faqs.question: Why will my EMF not open at all?
faqs.answer: A damaged record length can prevent a reader from locating the next drawing record.

faqs.question: Does trying this page send my EMF anywhere?
faqs.answer: No. Nothing leaves your device, and without an EMF reader in the browser the attempt just ends in an error.

faqs.question: Why would I want a PNG instead of an EMF?
faqs.answer: EMF is a Windows format that stores vector drawing commands and scales without loss. PNG is a lossless raster format that supports alpha transparency, and any browser can show it.

guide.title: About EMF files
guide.markdown:
### What is an EMF file?

EMF, Enhanced Metafile, is Microsoft's format for storing graphics as recorded drawing operations. Instead of pixels, the file holds a header, a series of drawing records and an end record. The records describe graphics objects, property changes and drawing orders.

Its device-independent design keeps drawing proportions across output devices. The first extension to the format added a pixel-format record and OpenGL command support. RFC 7903 identifies image/emf and the older image/x-emf media type.

EMF is used for charts and diagrams pasted into Office documents and for Windows printing and clipboard graphics. Bitmaps can be embedded too, so a single file may hold both kinds.

The target, PNG, is a lossless raster picture format. Created in the mid-1990s as a GIF successor free of patent trouble, PNG is covered by ISO standard 15948 and by a W3C Recommendation. It is used for screenshots and interface graphics, for logos and images with transparency, and for web graphics that must stay sharp. It has 8-bit and 16-bit channels.

### Programs that open EMF files

Microsoft Office and IrfanView also open EMF. Two more programs come from the fact sheet for EMF:

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- LibreOffice Draw: lists Enhanced Windows Metafile among its import formats.
- Inkscape: its format matrix lists EMF input and output support.

### EMF and PNG compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .emf with image/emf, or the older image/x-emf. The .png ending names a PNG, the lossless raster format.
- **Kind**: EMF stores drawing commands. PNG is a raster picture.
- **Scaling**: EMF scales without loss. A PNG has a fixed pixel size.
- **Compression**: PNG compression is lossless, so the pixels you export are kept exactly.
- **Transparency**: PNG supports alpha transparency.
- **Bitmaps**: an EMF can embed bitmaps, while a PNG is nothing but a bitmap.
- **Typical use**: EMF serves graphics inside Windows and Office. PNG is for screenshots, logos and sharp web graphics.
- **Support**: EMF is a Windows format that records Windows GDI drawing commands, while PNG is supported by every browser.

This page cannot do the conversion. It decodes images with the browser's own image decoder, and in a test that decoder could not read an EMF, so the attempt ends in an 'Image decode failed.' error. The file stays on your device and is not changed. Use one of the programs below. Both LibreOffice Draw and Inkscape run on Windows, Mac and Linux, so you do not need Windows to open an EMF.

LibreOffice Draw's guide names PNG among the graphics formats it exports. Check any imported result against the original. A browser works for viewing the exported PNG, as do GIMP, Windows Photos and Preview on macOS. Inkscape's wiki format matrix lists EMF among the formats it can both read and write, which is why it also appears in the list of programs above. A PNG from either program is a fixed grid of pixels, so export at the size you need, since enlarging the PNG later will not restore sharp edges.

### Other ways to convert EMF to PNG

- **ImageMagick on Windows:** run `magick office-diagram.emf office-diagram.png`. The command reads the EMF and writes a PNG. The ImageMagick formats page marks EMF as readable on Windows only, with the size option supported.
- **Inkscape (Windows, Mac, Linux):** open the EMF, press Shift+Ctrl+E or use File > Export PNG Image, choose the export area (Page, Drawing, Selection or Custom), set a size and a file name, and click Export.
- **LibreOffice Draw:** open the EMF, then export it as PNG. LibreOffice's guide gives no menu path for this.

### Problems with EMF files

- **A damaged file will not draw**: if a record length is damaged, the reader cannot find the next record.
- **A newer EMF looks wrong in an old program**: older EMF readers may not implement records introduced by the format's extensions.
- **Inkscape output differs from the original**: features Inkscape cannot import are lost, so compare the two.
- **Only part of a chart appears**: choose the Drawing export area in Inkscape instead of Page or Selection.
- **ImageMagick cannot read it on Mac or Linux**: EMF reading is listed as Windows only.
- **'Image decode failed.' shows on this page**: in a test the browser's decoder could not read the EMF.

seo.title: Convert GIF to AVI Online (Free)
seo.description: Convert an animated GIF to AVI in your browser. Frames are encoded as MPEG-4 (Xvid tag) in an AVI file, with frames capped at 1920 px and 30 fps. Free.

tool.subtitle: Turn an animated GIF into an AVI video with MPEG-4 video.

faqs.question: How do I convert GIF to AVI?
faqs.answer: Select the GIF, wait for the encode to finish and download the AVI. Queue more GIFs if you like; each yields its own AVI.

faqs.question: Which codec does the AVI use?
faqs.answer: MPEG-4 video, tagged xvid. The command also lists MP3 audio at 96 kbps, but a GIF has no sound to encode, and in a test run the AVI came out with no audio stream.

faqs.question: Does the AVI loop like the GIF?
faqs.answer: The page passes no loop setting, and the AVI is an ordinary video file, so use the repeat option in your player if you want it to loop. Keep the GIF where you need an endless loop.

faqs.question: Will the AVI look as sharp as the GIF?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. MPEG-4 is lossy and the page encodes at a fixed -q:v 10, so the AVI is not a pixel-exact copy of the GIF. The GIF itself loses nothing, but it is held to 256 colors in each frame.

faqs.question: What frame rate and size does the AVI have?
faqs.answer: A longer side over 1920 pixels is scaled down, while a smaller GIF keeps its size. Playback is held to 30 fps, and a faster GIF loses some frames but runs for the same time. Any odd dimension is trimmed by a pixel to become even.

faqs.question: Can the AVI come out larger than the GIF?
faqs.answer: Yes. In a test, a tiny GIF of 157 bytes became an AVI of 5,874 bytes. The size depends on the content, and the page sets no size target.

faqs.question: Does the AVI keep GIF transparency?
faqs.answer: No. One palette color in a GIF can be marked clear, but the AVI uses the yuv420p pixel format, and that format has no alpha, so transparent areas cannot stay transparent.

faqs.question: Can I choose the quality?
faqs.answer: No. The page uses a fixed setting and offers no slider. For a different quality, run FFmpeg yourself with another -q:v value.

faqs.question: Is my GIF uploaded?
faqs.answer: No. FFmpeg executes as WebAssembly in your browser, and the GIF stays on your device.

faqs.question: Can I drop in more than one GIF?
faqs.answer: Yes. Choose multiple GIFs and the page converts each in sequence. Every GIF becomes a separate AVI download, and no archive is built.

guide.title: About GIF files
guide.markdown:
### What is a GIF file?

CompuServe produced the Graphics Interchange Format in 1987; people call it GIF. It packs data with lossless LZW coding and gives each frame a palette of up to 256 colors. It also offers simple animation and 1-bit transparency.

A single GIF can hold several frames, which is how a simple animation is stored. Transparency here means one palette entry is declared fully clear, so there is no partial opacity. A disposal setting on each frame controls how the next image covers the one before it.

People use GIFs as brief looping animations, small graphics and icons, reaction images and stickers. The AVI side is a RIFF-based video container that arrived with Windows in 1992, and you meet it in video archives and legacy desktop editing.

### Programs that open GIF files

Any web browser, Preview on macOS, Windows Photos and GIMP open GIF files. Sorted by platform, the format's fact sheet names these:

**Windows, Mac and Linux**

- GIMP: writes still pictures or multilayer animations.
- ImageMagick: reads GIF; ask your install which formats it supports.

**Web and Mobile**

- Google Chrome: GIF display.

**Web**

- Mozilla Firefox: GIF display.

**Mobile**

- Safari: GIF display.

For the AVI you get, ffplay and mpv play it on Windows, Mac and Linux, Adobe Premiere opens AVI on Windows and Mac, and VLC plays it on Android and iOS.

### GIF and AVI compared

- **Extensions and media types**: .gif for GIF; .avi for AVI, commonly labeled video/x-msvideo.
- **Kind**: GIF is a raster image format with simple animation. AVI is a video container that can hold many different codecs.
- **Compression**: GIF uses lossless LZW with at most 256 colors per frame. The AVI from this page holds MPEG-4 video, which is lossy.
- **Looping**: GIFs are typically used as short looping animations. This page passes no loop setting to the AVI.
- **Transparency**: GIF has 1-bit transparency. The AVI is yuv420p video, and that pixel format carries no alpha.
- **Typical use**: GIFs are reaction images and stickers. AVI turns up in older Windows video, capture output and archives.

Inside your browser, a WebAssembly build of FFmpeg does the encoding. It writes MPEG-4 video tagged xvid at a fixed -q:v 10 with B-frames off, and MP3 at 96 kbps is named in the command as well. No GIF side goes past 1920 pixels, and a side that is odd gets trimmed by a pixel. The AVI never exceeds 30 fps, so a quicker GIF sheds frames but plays for the same length of time. No stream mapping is passed. The upload never happens, the GIF stays untouched, and the result is saved as the same name ending in .avi. With a batch of GIFs, the page converts them one after another, each into its own AVI. There is no cap on file size from this page.

### Other ways to convert GIF to AVI

- **FFmpeg (Windows, Mac, Linux):** run `ffmpeg -i reaction-loop.gif -c:v mpeg4 -q:v 5 reaction-clip.avi` for MPEG-4 video at a -q:v value you choose. FFmpeg's manual describes the -q:v scale as codec-dependent.
- **ImageMagick plus FFmpeg (command line):** run `magick diagram-motion.gif -coalesce diagram-frame-%04d.png`, then `ffmpeg -framerate 10 -i diagram-frame-%04d.png -c:v mpeg4 diagram-motion.avi` to control the frame rate yourself. The -coalesce option expands the frames into full images first.

### Problems with GIF files

- **Gradients look banded**: what GIMP writes as GIF is limited to 256 colors at most, so smooth gradients can shift.
- **Soft edges turn jagged**: a GIF cannot hold partial opacity along a soft transparent edge.
- **Frames overlap wrongly**: disposal choices determine what an earlier image leaves behind, so pick combine or replace to suit the animation.
- **A GIF comment is missing**: GIMP leaves out a comment containing characters beyond seven-bit ASCII.
- **Colors differ in the AVI**: lossy video at a fixed quality cannot match the GIF pixel for pixel.
- **The AVI is bigger than the GIF**: in a test, a tiny GIF became a larger AVI. The page sets no size target.
- **The AVI does not loop**: no loop setting is passed. Loop it in your player.
- **There is no sound**: the GIF is silent, and the test AVI had no audio stream.
- **An editor will not open the AVI**: an editor may recognize AVI but not include the decoder a given file needs. Play it in ffplay, mpv or VLC to check the file.
- **The speed looks different**: the AVI never runs above 30 fps, so a faster GIF loses frames and cannot be matched exactly.
